media.title: Yoga Clock
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Yoga Clock
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration (the free first try after the story video, before any concept video)
- Textbook source: Racing Seconds, the opening yoga story with its two wall clocks, read from the pictures as 05:35 a.m. and 05:55 a.m., and opening questions 1 to 3 (developer only). Activities 1 to 4 use the plan's own practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that the time spent is how far the long hand travels from the Start clock to the Finish clock, counted 5 minutes for each number.
- Out of scope: the 24-hour format, seconds, changing hours to minutes, noon and midnight, subtracting times in columns.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- Raghav's yoga room in the morning: a lavender wall, a wooden floor, a window with a low yellow sun, a yellow yoga mat (photo-style cut-out) with a flat drawing of Raghav standing on it, hands folded, as in the story.
- Two large wall clocks hang side by side with plates "Start" and "Finish". Both show 07:10 a.m. The Start clock is locked.
- Instruction line: "Raghav stopped at 07:40 a.m. How long did his yoga take?" The child is invited to tap a guess card, then turn the long hand of the Finish clock.
2. Scene and Objects
- Each clock is a code-drawn dial about 300 px across: teal rim, numbers 1 to 12, 60 small marks, blue short hand, orange long hand; the short hand creeps on as the long hand moves. Under it sit a time box ("07:10 a.m.") and a sun and moon switch, both hidden when the child reads the clocks (Activity 4 and the Challenge).
- Guided activities only: red labels 5, 10, 15 ... 60 ring each dial, one beside each number.
- A pale orange stretch grows on the Finish dial from the Start hand to the Finish hand (a thin outer ring after one full round). A "Time spent" card between the clocks shows "? minutes". Three guess cards sit under the clocks. Goal chips along the top: "Start", "Finish", "Time spent".
- The window shows the morning sun; in Activity 4 a dark sky with a moon.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the long hand of the Finish clock clockwise. It snaps to the 5-minute marks and, past 12, the short hand moves on by one hour. It cannot be turned back behind the Start (it springs back with a small shake) or past 11:55.
- In Activity 3 the child also sets the Start clock: drag the short hand to a number for the hour, the long hand for the minutes, and tap the sun or the moon.
- Answers use two small wheels, no typing: a time (hour 1 to 12, minutes 00 to 55) or a time spent (hours 0 to 3, minutes 0 to 55).
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" (puts the clocks back) and "Check", which becomes "Next" when the chips are green.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Raghav stopped at 07:40 a.m. How long did his yoga take?" Chips: "Start 07:10 a.m." (already green), "Finish 07:40 a.m.", "Time spent ?". Setup: Start locked at 07:10 a.m., minute labels on. Guess: the child taps "20 minutes", "30 minutes" or "40 minutes". The child turns the Finish long hand from 2 to 8 and a counter says 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Result: "30 minutes"; the matching guess card turns green with a bounce (another card only says "The stretch shows 30 minutes."). Why line: "From 2 to 8 is 6 numbers, and 6 × 5 = 30 minutes." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Raghav began at 09:35 a.m. and stopped at 10:10 a.m. How long was it?" Chips: "Start 09:35 a.m.", "Finish 10:10 a.m.", "Time spent ?". Setup: Start locked at 09:35 a.m., labels on. Guess cards: "25 minutes", "35 minutes", "45 minutes". The child turns the long hand from 7 past 12 to 2; the short hand moves on to just past 10. Result: "35 minutes". Why line: "09:35 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. is 60 − 35 = 25 minutes, and 10:00 a.m. to 10:10 a.m. is 10 minutes, so 25 + 10 = 35 minutes." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Set the clocks to 08:00 a.m. and 09:40 a.m. How long was it?" Chips: "Start 08:00 a.m.", "Finish 09:40 a.m.", "Time spent ?". Setup: both clocks at 06:00 a.m., no labels, counter hidden. Guess cards: "Less than 1 hour" and "More than 1 hour". The child sets the Start clock (short hand on 8), turns the Finish long hand once round and on to 8, sets "Time spent" with the wheels and presses Check. Result: "1 hour 40 minutes". Why line: "08:00 a.m. to 09:00 a.m. is 1 hour, and 09:00 a.m. to 09:40 a.m. is 40 minutes, so 1 hour 40 minutes." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent, reading). Goal line: "Read the two clocks. When did it start and finish, and how long was it?" Chips: "Start ?", "Finish ?", "Time spent ?". Setup: evening window with a moon; the tool sets Start (short hand just past 7, long hand on 3) and Finish (short hand just before 8, long hand on 11); no boxes, no labels. Guess cards: "Less than 30 minutes" and "More than 30 minutes". The child sets three answers with the wheels. Result: "07:15 p.m.", "07:55 p.m." and "40 minutes". Why line: "3 × 5 = 15 and 11 × 5 = 55, so 07:15 p.m. to 07:55 p.m. is 55 − 15 = 40 minutes." Help: independent.
- Practice: none.
- Star Challenge 1 (the story). Caption: "Raghav practices yoga in the morning." Goal lines, one at a time, in the book's words: "At what time did Raghav start practising Yoga?" then "At what time did he finish?" then "How much time did he spend practising Yoga?" Chips: "Start time", "Finish time", "Time spent". Setup: the two story clocks, hands only: Start has the short hand between 5 and 6 and the long hand on 7; Finish has the short hand just before 6 and the long hand on 11. Guess cards before the first question: "Less than 1 hour" and "More than 1 hour". The child answers with the wheels. Result: "05:35 a.m.", "05:55 a.m." and "20 minutes". Why line: "7 × 5 = 35 and 11 × 5 = 55, so 05:35 a.m. to 05:55 a.m. is 55 − 35 = 20 minutes." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The shaded stretch is the time that went by. Each number is 5 minutes, so counting the numbers in fives gives the minutes. Past 12 the short hand moves on by one hour, and one full round is 1 hour.
- Rules in the child's words: "The short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes." "Each number on the clock is 5 minutes." "The time spent is how far the long hand travels from the Start to the Finish."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the stretch glows, the activity pill gets a tick and the strip gives the why line. A wrong answer gives a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line. Retry is always free.
- Mistake: long hand on 7 read as 7 minutes -> "The 7 does not mean 7 minutes. Each number is 5 minutes: count 5, 10, 15 ... 35." The numbers light up from 12 to 7.
- Mistake: hour read from the wrong number (06:35 for the Start story clock) -> "The short hand has not reached 6 yet, so the hour is still 5." The short hand pulses.
- Mistake: counts the numbers, not the jumps (5 for 7 to 11) -> "Count the jumps between the numbers: from 7 to 11 is 4 jumps, and 4 × 5 = 20 minutes." The jumps pulse.
- Mistake: an hour in the time spent when the hand has not gone round -> "The long hand has not gone once round, so it is less than 1 hour." The stretch pulses.
- Mistake: a.m. or p.m. does not fit the window -> "The window is dark and the moon is out, so it is p.m." (story clocks: "Raghav practices yoga in the morning, so choose the sun."). Check pressed with the Finish still on the Start time -> "The Finish clock still shows the Start time. Turn its long hand forward."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Which hand shows the minutes? Count the numbers in fives." (2) visual clue: the numbers between the Start hand and the Finish hand light up one by one with 5, 10, 15 ... (3) almost the answer: the stretch is counted aloud in fives and the last number is replaced by "?" (story clocks: 5, 10, 15, "?").
- Edge cases: one full round (the hand back on its start number) is "1 hour", not 0 minutes, and the outer ring closes; a Finish equal to the Start is "0 minutes"; the long hand on 12 reads ":00"; minutes below 10 keep their zero ("09:05").
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when the Start time, the Finish time and the Time spent are all right. Hints are allowed.
- End screen: confetti falls here only. "Well done!" Remember: "The short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes." "Each number on the clock is 5 minutes." "The time spent is how far the long hand travels." Think and talk: "The long hand goes all the way round and stops on the same number. How much time went by?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: yoga room wall and floor (flat scene with a window, morning and evening versions); yellow yoga mat (photo-style cut-out); Raghav as flat drawings (standing, sitting cross-legged); wooden plates "Start" and "Finish"; sun and moon icons. The clocks, labels, stretch, outer ring and wheels are drawn in code.
- Language: English only. Times have a leading zero ("07:10 a.m."); durations are in words; no abbreviations.

tool_config.idea: Set a Start clock and a Finish clock, read the time on each, and read how much time lies between them from the shaded stretch that grows when the Finish minute hand moves forward.
tool_config.title: Yoga Clock
tool_config.screen: Raghav's yoga room, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a wooden floor, a yoga mat and, on the wall above it, two large analogue wall clocks side by side, named Start and Finish. The two clocks are the largest things on screen. Each clock has a dark teal rim, a pale face, every number from 1 to 12, 60 small marks, a blue hour hand and an orange minute hand, and the hour hand moves a little as the minute hand moves, like a real clock. Under each clock sits a digital read-out, hh:mm, with a switch beside it that shows a sun for a.m. and a moon for p.m. A pale orange shaded stretch grows on the Finish clock from the Start position to the Finish position as the student moves the Finish minute hand forward, and a stretch longer than 1 hour goes round again in a thin outer ring. Below the clocks a time spent box has two small number boxes, hours and minutes (the hours box can stay empty), with a large number pad and a Check button. Controls: drag the minute hand of either clock (the hour hand follows), tap the sun and moon switch of a clock, and type in the time spent box. On the cards where the tool sets the clocks, the digital read-outs are hidden and the student types the start time, the finish time and the time spent instead. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (resets the clocks of this card), Reset (returns both clocks to the start of the tool), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 6 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 6.
feedback: A wrong minute reading gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red. For the story's Start clock: the minute hand points at 7, so that is 7 × 5 = 35 minutes past.
A wrong hour reading says which hand to look at: the short blue hand shows the hour, and the hour is the number it has just passed, so between 5 and 6 the hour is 5.
A morning time typed with p.m. gets a note about the switch: the sun means a.m., the morning, and the moon means p.m., the afternoon or evening.
A solved card shows how the stretch was counted, for example: 09:35 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. is 25 minutes and 10:00 a.m. to 10:10 a.m. is 10 minutes, so 25 + 10 = 35 minutes.
A time spent that mixes up minutes and hours, such as 15 hours for 15 minutes, gets a note to look at the shaded stretch: if the minute hand has not gone round, the time is less than 1 hour.
tool_config.done_when: All 6 cards are done, the three answers about Raghav's yoga are read correctly from the clocks, and the last card is finished without a bottom-out hint.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): set the Start clock to 07:10 a.m. and the Finish clock to 07:40 a.m., then read the shaded stretch. How much time is between them? Answer: 30 minutes, because the minute hand moves from 2 to 8, that is 6 numbers, and 6 × 5 = 30 minutes.

Card 2 (practice values): set the Start clock to 09:35 a.m. and the Finish clock to 10:10 a.m. The shaded stretch passes the number 12. How much time is between them? Answer: 35 minutes, because 09:35 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. is 60 − 35 = 25 minutes, 10:00 a.m. to 10:10 a.m. is 10 minutes, and 25 + 10 = 35 minutes.

Card 3 (practice values): set the Start clock to 08:00 a.m. and the Finish clock to 09:15 a.m. The shaded stretch goes once round and a little more. How much time is between them? Answer: 1 hour 15 minutes, because 08:00 a.m. to 09:00 a.m. is 1 hour and 09:00 a.m. to 09:15 a.m. is 15 minutes.

Card 4 (practice values): set the Start clock to 06:20 a.m. and the Finish clock to 07:05 a.m. How much time is between them? Answer: 45 minutes, because 06:20 a.m. to 07:00 a.m. is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes, 07:00 a.m. to 07:05 a.m. is 5 minutes, and 40 + 5 = 45 minutes.

Card 5 (practice values): the tool sets the clocks for an evening. The Start clock has the hour hand between 7 and 8 and the minute hand on 3. The Finish clock has the hour hand between 7 and 8 and the minute hand on 11. Switch both to the moon, then type the start time, the finish time and the time spent. Answer: 07:15 p.m., 07:55 p.m. and 40 minutes, because 3 × 5 = 15, 11 × 5 = 55 and 55 − 15 = 40 minutes.

Challenge: 'Raghav practices yoga in the morning.' The two wall clocks of the story are shown with hands only: the first has the hour hand between 5 and 6 and the minute hand on 7, and the second has the hour hand just before 6 and the minute hand on 11. 'At what time did Raghav start practising Yoga? At what time did he finish? How much time did he spend practising Yoga?' The student reads both clocks and types the three answers. Answers: 05:35 a.m., 05:55 a.m. and 20 minutes, because 7 × 5 = 35, 11 × 5 = 55 and 55 − 35 = 20 minutes.

hint_ladder.text: Which hand tells the hour and which hand tells the minutes? Look at the short blue hand and the long orange hand.
Each number on the dial is 5 minutes. Count the minutes in fives from 12 to where the long hand points.
Look at the long orange hand on your clock: how many numbers past 12 is it? Multiply that number by 5 to get the minutes.
Worked step on a practice clock: the short hand is between 8 and 9, so the hour is 8. The long hand is on 4, and 4 × 5 = 20 minutes, so the time is 08:20. Do the same with your clock.

content.text:
Worked example: Zainab started colouring at 04:25 p.m. and stopped at 05:10 p.m. (a) How long did she colour? Then: (b) How long is it from 07:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m.?
1. (a) Hop to the next whole hour. 04:25 p.m. to 05:00 p.m. is 60 − 25 = 35 minutes.
2. 05:00 p.m. to 05:10 p.m. is 10 minutes.
3. 35 + 10 = 45 minutes, so Zainab coloured for 45 minutes.
4. (b) Hop whole hours first. 07:20 a.m. to 10:20 a.m. is 10 − 7 = 3 hours.
5. 10:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m. is 50 − 20 = 30 minutes.
6. So the time from 07:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m. is 3 hours 30 minutes.
7. Check: 07:20 a.m. plus 3 hours is 10:20 a.m., and 10:20 a.m. plus 30 minutes is 10:50 a.m.
Answer: (a) 45 minutes (b) 3 hours 30 minutes

6. 125 is the most and 85 is the least, so Mary is the longest and Remo is the least.

{{DIAGRAM:M1.S3.T3.C7.IMG1}}
1. Look at the first clock. The short blue hand is between $5$ and $6$, so the hour is $5$.
2. The long orange hand is on $7$. Each number on the dial is $5$ minutes.
3. $7 \times 5 = 35$ minutes.
4. The time is 05:35. Raghav practices yoga in the morning, so it is a.m.
[Image: Let us find out: Ans1: solution]
5. Check: the hour hand is between $5$ and $6$, so the time is after 05:00 and before 06:00, and 05:35 is in that stretch.
Answer: 05:35 a.m.
[Image: Let us find out: Ans1: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. Raghav started at 05:35 a.m. and finished at 05:55 a.m.
2. Both times are in the same hour, $5$, so take the smaller minutes from the bigger minutes.
3. $55 - 35 = 20$ minutes.
4. So Raghav spent $20$ minutes on yoga.
5. Check: 05:35 a.m. plus $20$ minutes is 05:55 a.m., because $35 + 20 = 55$.
Answer: $20$ minutes

content.text:
1. $(a)$: Both times are in the same hour, $1$, so take the smaller minutes from the bigger minutes.
2. $42 - 15 = 27$ minutes.
3. $(b)$: The minutes are the same, $18$, so count the hours.
4. $8 - 3 = 5$ hours.
5. $(c)$: Hop whole hours first. 09:15 a.m. to 11:15 a.m. is $11 - 9 = 2$ hours.
[Image: Let us find out: Ans4: solution]
6. 11:15 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. is $30 - 15 = 15$ minutes, so the answer to part $(c)$ is $2$ hours $15$ minutes.
7. Share your strategy: you can hop to the next whole hour, or count the hours first. Another strategy may also work.
8. Check: 01:15 p.m. plus $27$ minutes is 01:42 p.m., 03:18 p.m. plus $5$ hours is 08:18 p.m., and 09:15 a.m. plus $2$ hours $15$ minutes is 11:30 a.m.
Answer: $(a)$: $27$ minutes $(b)$: $5$ hours $(c)$: $2$ hours $15$ minutes. Your strategy may differ.

content.text:
1. Compare the hours first. Raghav has $1$ hour, Rani has $2$ hours and Ritu has $1$ hour.
2. Rani has the most hours, so Rani took the longest time.
3. Raghav and Ritu both have $1$ hour, so compare their minutes.
4. $20$ minutes is less than $35$ minutes, so Raghav took the least time.
[Image: Let us find out: Ans5: solution]
5. Check in minutes: Raghav $60 + 20 = 80$, Rani $120 + 10 = 130$ and Ritu $60 + 35 = 95$. The most is $130$ (Rani) and the least is $80$ (Raghav).
Answer: $(a)$: Rani, $2$ hours $10$ minutes $(b)$: Raghav, $1$ hour $20$ minutes

media.title: Day Strip
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Day Strip
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S4.T4.C18.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Racing Seconds, the 12-hour and 24-hour table, the match question and the trip to Nana ji's house, 08:00 hours to 09:05 hours (developer only). Activities 1 to 4 use practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that a p.m. time sits 12 boxes further along the day than its a.m. twin, so it adds 12 in the 24-hour format, and finds the time between two 24-hour times by hopping.
- Out of scope: adding or taking away a time (the Time Jumper does that), crossing noon or midnight, seconds.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A cork notice board in a school corridor, with a long cream timetable strip for one whole day pinned across it: the biggest thing on the stage, nearly as wide as the stage.
- It has 24 hour boxes numbered 00 to 23: 00 to 11 cream under a yellow sun (a.m.), 12 to 23 deep blue under a white moon (p.m.), with end flags "00:00" and "24:00". Guided activities add a tiny 12-hour name under each box ("3 p.m.", "noon").
- A red pin "First time" stands in box 01, threaded to a small clock above the strip. Read-out cards "12-hour" and "24-hour" sit below it.
- Instruction line: "Put the pin on 07:25 a.m., then on 03:40 p.m." The child is invited to tap a guess card first.
2. Scene and Objects
- Pins: "First time" (red) always; "Second time" (green) only in Activities 3 and 4 and Challenge 3. Each pin is threaded to its own small clock (about 110 px) with a blue short hand for the hour of its box and an orange long hand for the minutes.
- Read-out cards ("07:25 a.m.", "07:25 hours") are hidden when the child must write that time. A curved "+ 12" arrow joins a box to the box 12 places on. A gap bar joins the two pins and carries hop arcs.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a pin: it snaps to a whole-hour box from 01 to 23 (box 00 is greyed). Drag the long hand of its clock for the minutes (5-minute marks).
- Answers use wheels, no typing: 12-hour (hour 1 to 12, minutes 00 to 55, sun or moon switch), 24-hour (hour 00 to 23, minutes 00 to 55), time between (hours 0 to 5, minutes 0 to 55).
- In Challenges 1 and 2 cork-board cards replace the strip: tap a blank to write in it; in the match tap a left card and then a right card to pull a red string (a right pair stays pinned, a wrong pair springs back).
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and "Check", which becomes "Next" when the chips are green.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Put the pin on 07:25 a.m., then on 03:40 p.m." Chips: "07:25 a.m. ?" and "03:40 p.m. ?". Setup: pin in box 01, names and read-outs shown. Guess: "Which time keeps its digits in the 24-hour format?" (cards "07:25 a.m." and "03:40 p.m."). The child drags the pin to box 07 (long hand on 5), then to the box named "3 p.m." (box 15, long hand on 8); the +12 arrow draws from box 03 to box 15. Result: the read-outs say "07:25 hours" and "15:40 hours"; both chips turn green. Why line: "07:25 a.m. keeps its digits: 07:25 hours. 3 + 12 = 15, so 03:40 p.m. is 15:40 hours." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (independent). Goal line: "The 24-hour box says 21:20 hours. Write the 12-hour time." Chips: "21:20 hours" and "12-hour ?". Setup: pin already in box 21, long hand on 4; read-out and box names hidden. Guess: a sun card "A morning time" or a moon card "A p.m. time". The child writes the time with the wheels and presses Check. Result: "09:20 p.m.". Why line: "21 is more than 12, so it is p.m.: 21 − 12 = 9, and the minutes stay 20, so 21:20 hours is 09:20 p.m." Help: independent.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "How long is it from 09:25 hours to 11:50 hours?" Chips: "First 09:25 hours", "Second 11:50 hours", "Time between ?". Setup: pins in boxes 01 and 02, no 12-hour read-out. Guess: "Less than 2 hours" or "More than 2 hours". The child puts the pins on box 09 (long hand on 5) and box 11 (long hand on 10); hop arcs open, "2 hours" from 09:25 to 11:25 and "25 minutes" from 11:25 to 11:50. The child writes the time between. Result: "2 hours 25 minutes". Why line: "09:25 hours to 11:25 hours is 2 hours, and 11:25 hours to 11:50 hours is 25 minutes, so 2 hours 25 minutes." Help: guided.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "How long is it from 08:40 hours to 11:10 hours?" Chips: "First 08:40 hours", "Second 11:10 hours", "Time between ?". Setup as in Activity 3, no arcs. Guess: "Less than 3 hours" or "More than 3 hours". The child places both pins and writes the time between. Result: "2 hours 30 minutes", and the arcs draw themselves. Why line: "08:40 hours to 09:00 hours is 20 minutes, 09:00 hours to 11:00 hours is 2 hours, and 11:00 hours to 11:10 hours is 10 minutes, so 20 + 10 = 30 minutes and the time between is 2 hours 30 minutes." Help: independent.
- Practice: none.
- Star Challenge 1 (the table). Goal line: "Fill in the blanks by writing the time in the appropriate format." Chip: "4 blanks". Setup: a cork-board table, columns "Time in 12-hour format" and "Time in 24-hour format", a small digital clock "24:00" above the second. Rows: 05:30 a.m. and 05:30 hours; blank and 08:35 hours; 11:55 a.m. and blank; 02:30 p.m. and 14:30 hours; 05:30 p.m. and blank; 09:35 p.m. and blank. Guess (before each blank): "Keep the digits", "Add 12 to the hour" or "Take 12 away from the hour"; then the child writes the time with the wheels. Results: "08:35 a.m.", "11:55 hours", "17:30 hours", "21:35 hours". Why lines: "08 is less than 12, so 08:35 hours is a morning time: 08:35 a.m." "11:55 a.m. keeps its digits: 11:55 hours." "5 + 12 = 17, so 05:30 p.m. is 17:30 hours." "9 + 12 = 21, so 09:35 p.m. is 21:35 hours." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (the match). Goal line: "Match the following." Chip: "6 matches". Setup: two columns of six paper cards. Left, "Time in 12-hour format": 06:30 a.m., 08:45 p.m., 11:45 p.m., 04:30 a.m., 07:30 p.m., 01:30 a.m. Right, "Time in 24-hour format": 01:30 hours, 23:45 hours, 06:30 hours, 20:45 hours, 04:30 hours, 19:30 hours. Guess: "Tap the three morning times first." (a tap on a p.m. card says "That one is p.m., so it comes after noon."). Then the child pulls a string for each pair. Result: six strings stay. Why line: "Morning times keep their digits. For p.m. times, 8 + 12 = 20, 11 + 12 = 23 and 7 + 12 = 19." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (the trip). Goal line: "Raghu left his house at 08:00 hours and arrived at his Nana ji's house at 09:05 hours. How long did he take to reach his house?" Chip: "Time taken ?". Setup: the strip returns, pins in boxes 01 and 02. Guess: "Less than 1 hour" or "More than 1 hour". The child puts the pins on box 08 (long hand on 12) and box 09 (long hand on 1), then writes the time between. Result: "1 hour 5 minutes". Why line: "08:00 hours to 09:00 hours is 1 hour, and 09:00 hours to 09:05 hours is 5 minutes, so Raghu took 1 hour 5 minutes." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A p.m. time sits exactly 12 boxes further along than its a.m. twin, and the "+ 12" arrow shows it. A morning time has no jump, so it keeps its digits. For a gap there is no a.m. or p.m. to track: hop to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the activity pill gets a tick and the strip shows the why line. A wrong answer gives a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line. Retry is free.
- Mistake: a p.m. time keeps its digits (05:30 hours for 05:30 p.m.) -> "A p.m. time adds 12 to the hour. Look 12 boxes further on from 5." The +12 arrow draws from box 05 to box 17.
- Mistake: a morning time gets 12 added (19:25 for 07:25 a.m.) -> "A morning time keeps its digits. The pin is on the sun side." 21:20 hours written as a morning time -> "21 is more than 12, so the pin is on the moon side: it is p.m." The minutes changed (09:25 p.m.) -> "The minutes never change: 20 stays 20." The sun or moon side pulses.
- Mistake: only the hours counted (2 hours for 09:25 hours to 11:50 hours) -> "Count the minutes left too: how far is it from 11:25 hours to 11:50 hours?" Digits taken away (3 hours 30 minutes for 08:40 hours to 11:10 hours) -> "Hop to the next whole hour first: how many minutes from 08:40 hours to 09:00 hours?"
- Mistake in the match: a morning card joined to different digits -> "A morning time keeps its digits. Look for the same hour and minutes." A p.m. card joined to a card under 12 -> "A p.m. time adds 12 to the hour."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Is it a morning time or a p.m. time? Or are you finding the time between?" (2) visual clue: the +12 arrow appears (backwards for 24-hour times above 12) and the sun or moon side glows; for a gap two hop arcs appear, numbers hidden; in Challenge 1 a small strip appears above the table. (3) almost the answer: the arrow shows the hour and "+ 12" with the answer "?"; the arcs show every number but the last.
- Edge cases: a time on the hour has the long hand on 12 and reads ":00"; minutes below 10 keep their zero; two pins on the same time show "0 minutes".
7. Ending
- Each star is done when its answers are right. Hints are allowed.
- End screen: confetti falls here only. "Well done!" Remember: "A morning time keeps its digits in the 24-hour format." "For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour. The minutes never change." "To find the time between, hop to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest." Think and talk: "Why does the 24-hour format never need a.m. or p.m.?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: cork notice board (photo-style); cream paper strip of 24 boxes (a.m. boxes cream, p.m. boxes deep blue); sun and moon cut-outs; red and green pins; paper cards with red string; small digital clock "24:00". Clocks, arrows, arcs and wheels are drawn in code.
- Language: English only; times have a leading zero; durations are in words.

tool_config.screen: The school notice board, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A long timetable strip for one whole day is pinned across the board and is the largest thing on screen. The strip has 24 hour boxes numbered 00 to 23 from left to right, the a.m. side (00 to 11) under a sun and the p.m. side (12 to 23) under a moon, with the two ends labelled 00:00 and 24:00. Two draggable markers sit on the strip, named First time and Second time, and each marker has a small analogue clock above it (blue hour hand, orange minute hand, 60 small marks) that follows the marker. Two read-outs sit under the strip for the selected marker: the 12-hour read-out, hh:mm a.m. or p.m., and the 24-hour read-out, hh:mm hours. A gap bar between the two markers shows the time between them in hours and minutes. Controls: drag a marker along the strip (it snaps to 5 minutes and stays between 01:00 hours and 23:55 hours), tap a read-out to type a time with a large number pad, a switch named Show the 12 added that draws a +12 bracket over the p.m. side, and a Check button. On a gap card the 12-hour read-out is hidden, because the gap is read in 24-hour time. For the book's match question the strip is replaced by two columns of boxes and the student taps a 12-hour time and then its 24-hour time to draw a line between them. feedback: A wrong 24-hour time for a p.m. time gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red, and the +12 bracket lights up: for 05:30 p.m., the hour 5 plus 12 is 17, the minutes stay 30, so 17:30 hours.
A morning time shows its twin: the note points to the a.m. side of the strip and shows the same hour box under the marker, so 07:45 a.m. is 07:45 hours.
A 24-hour time above 12 typed as a morning time gets a note: 21 is more than 12, so the marker is in the moon side of the strip, and 21 − 12 = 9 gives 09:20 p.m.
A wrong gap shows the hops on the gap bar, to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest, with the numbers written on the bar.
A gap typed with minutes above 59 gets a note: minutes on a clock never go past 59, so recount with the hops on the bar.

It adds a.m. or p.m. A day has 24 hours, so the 12-hour clock goes round twice. The first round is the morning (a.m.). The second round is the afternoon and evening (p.m.). The 24-hour format counts once, from 00:00 to 24:00. It does not use a.m. or p.m. It writes the word hours after the time. A morning time keeps its digits: 05:30 a.m. is 05:30 hours. For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour: 02:30 p.m. is 2 + 12 = 14, so it is 14:30 hours. The minutes never change. To go back from a 24-hour time above 12, take 12 away from the hour. Rule: a morning time keeps its digits. For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour. The minutes stay the same. 1. (a) 07:45 p.m. is a p.m. time, so add 12 to the hour. 2. 7 + 12 = 19. 3. The minutes stay 45, so 07:45 p.m. is 19:45 hours. 4. (b) 16 is more than 12, so it is a p.m. time. Take 12 away from the hour. 5. 16 − 12 = 4. 6. The minutes stay 20, so 16:20 hours is 04:20 p.m. 7. Check: going back, 4 + 12 = 16 and 19 − 12 = 7, so both answers match. Answer: (a) 19:45 hours (b) 04:20 p.m.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Raghu's art class starts at 15:20 hours and ends at 17:05 hours. Is it longer than 2 hours or shorter than 2 hours? Shorter. With 24-hour times there is no a.m. or p.m. to keep track of, so just count up from the earlier time to the later time. Hop to the next whole hour: 15:20 hours to 16:00 hours is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes. Hop whole hours: 16:00 hours to 17:00 hours is 17 − 16 = 1 hour. Add the rest: 17:00 hours to 17:05 hours is 5 minutes. 40 + 5 = 45 minutes, so the class lasts 1 hour 45 minutes. That is shorter than 2 hours. Hop in your head instead of subtracting in columns, because an hour has 60 minutes and not 100. Rule: go to the next whole hour, add the whole hours, then add the rest of the minutes. 1. 13:40 hours to 14:00 hours is 60 − 40 = 20 minutes. 2. 14:00 hours to 16:00 hours is 16 − 14 = 2 hours. 3. 16:00 hours to 16:15 hours is 15 minutes. 4. 20 + 15 = 35 minutes. 5. So the drawing class lasts 2 hours 35 minutes. 6. Check: 13:40 hours plus 2 hours is 15:40 hours, and 15:40 hours plus 35 minutes is 16:15 hours. Answer: 2 hours 35 minutes

content.text:
Worked example: (a) Write 07:45 p.m. in the 24-hour format. (b) Write 16:20 hours in the 12-hour format.
1. (a) 07:45 p.m. is a p.m. time, so add 12 to the hour.
2. 7 + 12 = 19.
3. The minutes stay 45, so 07:45 p.m. is 19:45 hours.
4. (b) 16 is more than 12, so it is a p.m. time. Take 12 away from the hour.
5. 16 − 12 = 4.
6. The minutes stay 20, so 16:20 hours is 04:20 p.m.
7. Check: going back, 4 + 12 = 16 and 19 − 12 = 7, so both answers match.
Answer: (a) 19:45 hours (b) 04:20 p.m.

concepts.concept_name: Two Ways to Write the Time

content.text:
1. Predict first: Raghu's art class starts at 15:20 hours and ends at 17:05 hours. Is it longer than 2 hours or shorter than 2 hours?
2. Shorter. With 24-hour times there is no a.m. or p.m. to keep track of, so just count up from the earlier time to the later time.
3. Hop to the next whole hour: 15:20 hours to 16:00 hours is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes.
4. Hop whole hours: 16:00 hours to 17:00 hours is 17 − 16 = 1 hour.
5. Add the rest: 17:00 hours to 17:05 hours is 5 minutes. 40 + 5 = 45 minutes, so the class lasts 1 hour 45 minutes. That is shorter than 2 hours.
6. Hop in your head instead of subtracting in columns, because an hour has 60 minutes and not 100.
7. Rule: go to the next whole hour, add the whole hours, then add the rest of the minutes.

content.text:
Worked example: In a race, Remo's time is 01:48 and Zainab's time is 01:52, in minutes and seconds. Read each time. Who won, and by how many seconds? Change Remo's time to seconds.
1. 01:48 means 1 minute 48 seconds. 01:52 means 1 minute 52 seconds.
2. Both took 1 minute, so compare the seconds. 48 is less than 52.
3. The least time wins, so Remo won.
4. 52 − 48 = 4 seconds, so Remo won by 4 seconds.
5. 1 minute = 60 seconds, so 1 minute 48 seconds = 60 + 48 = 108 seconds.
6. Check: Zainab's 1 minute 52 seconds is 60 + 52 = 112 seconds, and 112 − 108 = 4 seconds.
Answer: Remo won by 4 seconds. His time, 1 minute 48 seconds, is 108 seconds

content.text:
1. Predict first: would you measure blinking your eyes in seconds or in minutes? And melting an ice-cube?
2. 1 minute is 60 seconds. Blinking is over in a moment, far less than 1 minute, so use seconds. Melting an ice-cube takes much longer than 1 minute, so use minutes.
3. Ask one question: is it over in less than 1 minute? If yes, use seconds. If it takes longer than 1 minute, use minutes.
4. This is an estimate, so your answer may be a little different from a friend's answer.
5. Rule: less than 1 minute, use seconds. More than 1 minute, use minutes.

content.publication_text: Find out the number of times you can skip the rope in $10$ seconds.

content.text:
1. Ask a friend to watch the seconds hand. Begin when it is on $12$ and stop when it is on $2$.
2. From $12$ to $2$ is $2 \times 5 = 10$ seconds.
3. Count how many times you skip in that time.
4. Sample answer (practice values): $14$ skips in $10$ seconds.
5. In $1$ minute there are $6$ times $10$ seconds, so you would skip about $14 \times 6 = 84$ times.
6. Check: $10 \times 6 = 60$, so $6$ times $10$ seconds is $1$ minute. Your answer may differ.
Answer: Sample answer (practice values): $14$ skips in $10$ seconds. Your answer may differ

media.title: Seconds Clock
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Seconds Clock
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S12.T12.C46.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Racing Seconds, the four pairs of clocks (Rani, Raghav, Ritu, Raghu) and the four draw-the-seconds-hand pairs (20, 30, 60 and 40 seconds) (developer only). Activities 1 to 4 use practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that each number on the dial is 5 seconds, that the red hand takes 60 seconds to go once round, and that the long hand moves on by one mark each time it does.
- Out of scope: changing seconds to minutes and seconds (the Time Converter Line does that), hours, anything shorter than a second.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The timing board beside the school track: a red-brown running track with white lane lines and a small "200 m" signpost (flat drawing, as in the race picture). In front, a wooden post carries one very large clock that fills most of the stage height: teal rim, numbers 1 to 12, 60 small marks, blue short hand, orange long hand and a thin red seconds hand. The hands read 04:20; the red hand is on 2.
- A round red "Run" button sits on the post under the clock. Small red labels 5, 10 ... 60 ring the dial.
- Instruction line: "The red hand starts on 2 and stops on 11. How many seconds?" The child is invited to tap a guess card.
2. Scene and Objects
- A pale red copy of the red hand, the start ghost, stays on the start number; a pale red stretch fills the dial from the ghost to the red hand. A "Seconds counted" box shows the count. A small step light beside the 12 blinks when the red hand passes 12, and the long hand then moves on by one mark. The labels and the counter show only in guided activities.
- For the book's pairs two clocks stand side by side (each as large as the stage allows), a left clock and a right clock, with the sentence and a "___ seconds" box below.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the red hand: it snaps to the numbers. The stretch is always measured clockwise from the start ghost; the hand dropped back on the start shows 0.
- "Run" (only on cards that say how many seconds): the red hand moves one number every beat, slowly enough to watch, passes 12 if it must, and stops by itself.
- The answer is a small box with "−" and "+" buttons in steps of 5, from 0 to 60. No typing.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and "Check", which becomes "Next" when the chip is green.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "The red hand starts on 2 and stops on 11. How many seconds?" Chip: "2 to 11". Setup: hand and ghost on 2, labels on. Guess: "9 seconds", "45 seconds" or "55 seconds". The child drags the hand to 11 and the counter climbs in fives. Result: "45 seconds". Why line: "2 is 10 seconds and 11 is 55 seconds, and 55 − 10 = 45 seconds." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "The red hand starts on 7 and stops on 3. How many seconds?" Chip: "7 to 3". Setup: hand and ghost on 7, labels on. Guess: "It passes 12" or "It does not pass 12". The child drags the hand clockwise past 12 to 3; the step light blinks and the long hand moves on by one mark. Result: "40 seconds". Why line: "7 is 35 seconds, 35 to 60 is 60 − 35 = 25 seconds, and 12 to 3 is 15 seconds, so 25 + 15 = 40 seconds." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "The red hand is on 8. It runs for 45 seconds. Where does it stop?" Chip: "Run 45 seconds". Setup: hand on 8, no labels, no counter. Guess: the child drags a pale guess hand to where the red hand will stop, then presses "Run": the hand moves 9 numbers, passes 12 and stops on 5; the guess hand turns green if it is on 5 (otherwise the strip says "It stopped on 5."). Why line: "8 is 40 seconds, 40 + 45 = 85, and 85 − 60 = 25 seconds, so the hand stops on 5 and the long hand moves on by one mark." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "The red hand is on 2. Run it for 60 seconds. Where does it stop?" Chip: "Run 60 seconds". Setup and guess as in Activity 3. Result: one full round; the hand is back on 2 and the long hand has moved on by one mark. Why line: "60 seconds is one full round, so the red hand is back on 2 and the long hand moves on by one mark." Help: independent.
- Practice: none.
- Star Challenge 1 (reading the pairs). Goal line: "Observe the clocks and fill in the blanks." Chip: "4 clocks". Four pairs, one after another: 1 "Rani took ___ seconds to get out of her bed." (red hand on 12, then on 6; short hands between 6 and 7, long hands on 9). 2 "Raghav took ___ seconds to move from his room to the kitchen." (12, then 7; short hand on 4, long hand on 9). 3 "Ritu took ___ seconds to pick up a piece of paper from the floor." (9, then 12; short hands between 5 and 6, long hands on 6). 4 "Raghu took ___ seconds to wash his spoon and plate." (5 and 5; short hand on 6; the right clock's long hand one mark on). Guess: "Did the long hand move on between the two clocks?" ("Yes" or "No"). The child sets the seconds with "−" and "+" and presses Check. Answers: 30, 35, 15 and 60 seconds. Why lines: "From 12 to 6 is 6 numbers, and 6 × 5 = 30 seconds." "From 12 to 7 is 7 numbers, and 7 × 5 = 35 seconds." "9 is 45 seconds and 12 is 60 seconds, and 60 − 45 = 15 seconds." "The red hand went once round and is back on 5, and the long hand moved on, so it took 60 seconds." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (drawing the hand). Goal line: "Draw the missing seconds hand on the clock on the right side." Chip: "4 clocks". Four pairs, the right clock with no red hand: 1 "Raghu took 20 seconds to read a sentence in his book." (short hands between 6 and 7, long hands on 9; left red hand on 12). 2 "Rani took 30 seconds to colour a rectangle." (short hands on 4, long hands on 9; on 12). 3 "Raghav took 60 seconds to move from his home to the garden." (short hands between 5 and 6, long hand on 6; on 9). 4 "Ritu took 40 seconds to wash a plate." (short hands on 6, long hands on 12; on 11). Guess: "Will the hand pass 12?" ("Yes" or "No"). The child drags a red hand onto the right clock and presses Check. Answers: on 4; on 6; on 9 again; on 7 (in 3 and 4 the tool draws the long hand one mark on). Why lines: "20 ÷ 5 = 4, so the hand goes 4 numbers on from 12 and stops on 4." "30 ÷ 5 = 6, so the hand stops on 6." "9 is 45 seconds, 45 + 60 = 105 and 105 − 60 = 45, so the hand is on 9 again and the long hand moves on by one mark." "11 is 55 seconds, 55 + 40 = 95 and 95 − 60 = 35, and 35 ÷ 5 = 7, so the hand stops on 7 and the long hand moves on by one mark." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The numbers on the dial go in steps of 5 seconds, so moving the red hand from one number to another is counting in fives. Passing 12 means the hand has gone once round: the count carries on and the long hand moves on by one mark. One full round is 60 seconds, which is 1 minute.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the stretch glows, the activity pill gets a tick and the strip gives the why line. A wrong answer gives a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line. Retry is free.
- Mistake: the number on the dial given as the seconds (6 for 12 to 6) -> "The 6 is not 6 seconds. Each number is 5 seconds: 6 × 5 = 30." The labels light up.
- Mistake: the numbers are taken away when the hand passes 12 (the child works out 7 − 3 for 7 to 3) -> "The hand went past 12. Count to 12 first and then on: 7 to 12, then 12 to 3." The path past 12 glows.
- Mistake: the same number at the start and the end means 0 seconds (Raghu, 5 and 5) -> "Look at the long hand: it moved on, so the red hand went once round. That is 60 seconds." The long hand pulses.
- Mistake in drawing: the seconds used as the number (the hand on 20) -> "The numbers go 1 to 12. 20 seconds is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 numbers on from 12."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Which hand is the seconds hand? It is the thin red one. Each number is 5 seconds." (2) visual clue: the labels 5, 10 ... 60 appear if hidden and light up one by one from the start to the stop. (3) almost the answer: the start and the stop are written in seconds (for example "8 is 40 seconds") and the last step is "?".
- Edge cases: 12 is 0 seconds at the start and 60 seconds at the end (9 to 12 is 15 seconds); a run that ends exactly on 12 also moves the long hand on.
7. Ending
- Each star is done when its four answers are right. Hints are allowed.
- End screen: confetti falls here only. "Well done!" Remember: "Each number on the clock is 5 seconds." "One full round of the red hand is 60 seconds, and the long hand moves on by one mark." "If the red hand goes past 12, count to 12 first and then on." Think and talk: "The red hand starts on 4 and stops on 4 again. Can that be 0 seconds? What do you look at?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: school running track with lane lines and a "200 m" signpost (flat drawing); wooden post (photo-style cut-out); round red button. Clocks, labels, stretch, ghost hands, step light and counter are drawn in code.
- Language: English only; the hands are "the red hand" and "the long hand".

tool_config.idea: Run the seconds hand, mark where it started, and read how many seconds have passed from the numbers it moved over, five seconds for each number; then drag the seconds hand to the place where it stops after a given number of seconds, and see the minute hand step on when the hand goes once round.
tool_config.title: Seconds Clock
tool_config.screen: The timing board beside the school track, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a post with one very large analogue clock on it, the largest thing on screen, with a dark teal rim, a pale face, every number from 1 to 12, 60 small marks, a short blue hour hand, a long orange minute hand and a thin red seconds hand. A ring of small labels 5, 10, 15, ..., 60 sits just outside the dial, one label beside each number. A pale copy of the seconds hand, named the start ghost, stays where the run began. A pale red stretch is shaded round the dial from the start ghost to the seconds hand. A box named Seconds counted shows the number of seconds, and a small step light beside the minute hand blinks when the seconds hand passes 12 and the minute hand moves on by one mark. Controls: Go (the seconds hand runs, one mark at a time, at a slow speed so it can be watched) and Stop, Mark start, a button Run for N seconds on the cards that say how many seconds, drag the seconds hand with a finger, type a number of seconds with a large number pad, and Check. On the book's cards two clocks sit side by side, a left clock and a right clock, as in the pictures, and the student types the seconds taken or drags the missing seconds hand onto the right clock. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (returns the hand to the start of this card), Reset (returns the clock to 12), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 7 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 7.
feedback: The seconds taken are shown on the stretch as the hand moves, so the student sees the count grow in fives: 5, 10, 15, and the Seconds counted box gives the same number.
A wrong number of seconds gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red: from 9 to 12 the hand passes 3 numbers, so 3 × 5 = 15 seconds, and the stretch is shaded on the clock.

A hand dragged to the wrong number is not moved back by the tool: the stretch from the start to the dragged hand is shaded and its seconds are written, and the student sees that they do not match the seconds asked for.
When the hand goes past 12 the step light blinks and a note says that the minute hand moves on by one mark each time the seconds hand goes once round, and that 60 seconds is 1 minute.
A hand on the same number at the start and the end gets a note to look at the minute hand: if it has moved on by one mark, one full round has passed, which is 60 seconds.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are done, the four seconds taken and the four drawn hands of the book are correct, and the last card is finished without a bottom-out hint.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 12. Press Go and press Stop when the hand is on 3. How many seconds have passed? Answer: 15 seconds, because each number is 5 seconds and 3 × 5 = 15.

Card 2 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 2. Mark the start, press Go and press Stop on 11. How many seconds? Answer: 45 seconds, because 2 is 10 seconds, 11 is 55 seconds and 55 − 10 = 45.

Card 3 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 10 and stops on 4, after it has gone past 12. Watch the step light. How many seconds? Answer: 30 seconds, because from 10 to 12 is 60 − 50 = 10 seconds, from 12 to 4 is 4 × 5 = 20 seconds, and 10 + 20 = 30 seconds. The minute hand moved on by one mark.

Card 4 (practice values): the seconds hand is on 7. It runs for 40 seconds. Drag the seconds hand to where it stops and say what the minute hand does. Answer: on 3, because 7 is 35 seconds, 35 + 40 = 75, 75 − 60 = 15 seconds, and 15 ÷ 5 = 3; the hand went past 12 once, so the minute hand moves on by one mark.

Card 5 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 5. Press Run for 60 seconds. Where does the hand stop and what happens to the minute hand? Answer: the hand is back on 5 and the minute hand has moved on by one mark, because one full round is 60 seconds, which is 1 minute.

(on 9 and then on 12), 'Raghu took ___ seconds to wash his spoon and plate.' (on 5 both times, with the minute hand one mark on). Answers: 30 seconds, 35 seconds, 15 seconds and 60 seconds.

Challenge: 'Draw the missing seconds hand on the clocks on the right side.' Four pairs of clocks, the right clock of each with no seconds hand: 'Raghu took 20 seconds to read a sentence in his book.' (the left hand on 12), 'Rani took 30 seconds to color a rectangle.' (on 12), 'Raghav took 60 seconds to move from his home to the garden.' (on 9), 'Ritu took 40 seconds to wash a plate.' (on 11). Answers: the hand on 4, on 6, on 9 again with the minute hand one mark on, and on 7 with the minute hand one mark on.

Worked step on a practice clock: the hand goes from 4 to 9. 4 × 5 = 20 seconds and 9 × 5 = 45 seconds, and 45 − 20 = 25 seconds. Do the same with the numbers on your card.

(on 9 and then on 12), 'Raghu took ___ seconds to wash his spoon and plate.' (on 5 both times, with the minute hand one mark on). Answers: 30 seconds, 35 seconds, 15 seconds and 60 seconds.

(the left hand on 12), 'Rani took 30 seconds to color a rectangle.' (on 12), 'Raghav took 60 seconds to move from his home to the garden.' (on 9), 'Ritu took 40 seconds to wash a plate.' (on 11). Answers: the hand on 4, on 6, on 9 again with the minute hand one mark on, and on 7 with the minute hand one mark on.

content.text:
Worked example: The seconds hand is on 10. It runs for 25 seconds. Where does it stop, and what happens to the minute hand?
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S12.T12.C45.IMG2}}
1. The hand starts on 10. Each number is 5 seconds, so 10 is 10 × 5 = 50 seconds.
2. 50 + 25 = 75 seconds.
3. 75 is more than 60, so the hand has gone past 12 once. 75 − 60 = 15 seconds.
4. 15 seconds is 15 ÷ 5 = 3, so the hand stops on 3.
5. The hand went past 12 once, so the minute hand has moved on by one mark.
6. Check: from 10 to 12 is 10 seconds and from 12 to 3 is 15 seconds, and 10 + 15 = 25 seconds.
Answer: The seconds hand stops on 3, and the minute hand moves on by one mark

1. The seconds hand is on $5$ in both clocks, which is $5 \times 5 = 25$ seconds.
2. The minute hand in the right clock has moved on by one mark since the left clock.
3. So the seconds hand went once round the clock and came back to $5$. One full round is $60$ seconds.
4. Check: $60$ movements of the seconds hand make the minute hand move on by one minute, and $1$ minute is $60$ seconds.
Answer: $60$ seconds ($1$ minute)

media.title: Time Converter Line
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Time Converter Line
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S14.T14.C65.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Racing Seconds, Zainab and Remo's talk and Let Us Do 1 (a), (b), (c) and 2 with the two double number lines (developer only). Activities 1 to 3 use practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that on a double number line each step to the smaller unit multiplies by 60, and that going back means finding how many whole groups of 60 fit and keeping what is left.
- Out of scope: units bigger than hours or smaller than seconds, a.m. and p.m., finding the time between two times.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- Raghav's homework table: a dark wooden desk seen from slightly above, with a lamp, a pencil box and a notebook at the edges. A long cream paper tape across it, the biggest thing on the stage (nearly the full stage width), carries two aligned lines: a top line with blue ticks (the bigger unit) and a bottom line with orange ticks (the smaller unit), each top tick above a bottom tick.
- Mode "Hours and minutes": top line 0 to 12 hours, bottom line 0 to 720 minutes, a tick for each hour; a curved arrow "× 60" joins 1 hour to 60 minutes. A clear ruler with a brass handle, the slider, stands on 0 across both lines. A sticker switch at the left end reads "Hours and minutes" or "Minutes and seconds".
- Instruction line: "How many minutes is 3 hours 50 minutes?" The child is invited to tap a guess card first.
2. Scene and Objects
- Two tags under the slider show its number on each line; they and the "× 60" arrow show only in guided activities.
- A groups-of-60 strip under the bottom line: blocks each worth 60 and a short block for what is left; it appears with Hint level 2 or once an answer is solved. An orange end-piece can be pulled along the bottom line from a whole top tick to add extra minutes (or seconds).
- Mode "Minutes and seconds": top line 0 to 25 minutes, bottom line 0 to 1500 seconds.
- Challenge 3 only: four books on the desk (Mathematics, English, Hindi, The World Around Us), each tagged "50 minutes".
3. Main Interaction
- Drag the slider: it snaps to a whole number on the top line. In the challenges it is locked.
- Tap a blank: a small number pad (0 to 9, back, OK; at most 3 digits) opens, one blank at a time.
- Tap a block of the strip to cut it off: it becomes 1 on the top line and the short block shows what is left.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and "Check", which becomes "Next" when the chips are green.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "How many minutes is 3 hours 50 minutes?" Chip: "3 hours 50 minutes". Setup: Hours and minutes, arrow and tags on. Guess: "150 minutes", "230 minutes" or "350 minutes". The child slides to 3 hours (bottom tag 180), drags the orange end-piece on by 50 minutes and types the total. Result: "230 minutes". Why line: "3 hours is 3 × 60 = 180 minutes, and 180 + 50 = 230 minutes." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (independent). Goal line: "470 minutes: how many hours and minutes?" Chip: "470 minutes". Setup: bottom slider on 470, tags and strip hidden. Guess: "Between 6 and 7 hours", "Between 7 and 8 hours" or "Between 8 and 9 hours". The child types the hours and the minutes. Result: "7 hours 50 minutes"; the strip shows 7 blocks and a short block of 50. Why line: "60 × 7 = 420 and 470 − 420 = 50, so 470 minutes is 7 hours 50 minutes." Help: independent.
- Activity 3 (guided, second mode). Goal line: "How many seconds is 9 minutes 40 seconds?" Chip: "9 minutes 40 seconds". Setup: Minutes and seconds, arrow and tags on. Guess: "49 seconds", "580 seconds" or "940 seconds". The child slides to 9 minutes (tag 540), drags the end-piece on by 40 seconds and types the total. Result: "580 seconds". Why line: "9 minutes is 9 × 60 = 540 seconds, and 540 + 40 = 580 seconds." Help: guided.
- Practice: none.
- Star Challenge 1 (hours and minutes). Goal line: "Use the double number line below to complete the conversions." Chip: "7 blanks". Setup: slider locked. Top line: 1 hour, ___, 4 hours, 7 hours, ___, 9 hours, ___, ___. Bottom line: 60 minutes, 120 minutes, ___, ___, 480 minutes, ___, 660 minutes, 720 minutes (ticks at 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 hours; a "× 2" arrow joins 1 hour to the second tick). Guess: "Each hour adds how many minutes?" ("60", "100" or "10"). The child fills the blanks with the pad. Answers: hours 2, 8, 11, 12; minutes 240, 420, 540. Why line: "1 hour is 60 minutes, so 4 × 60 = 240, 7 × 60 = 420 and 9 × 60 = 540." Then the goal line becomes "Do as instructed. You can use the above double number line for the following conversions." Chip: "8 conversions". One at a time; each guess is a tap on the stretch of the bottom line where the answer will land. Items and answers: (i) 1 hour 10 minutes = ___ minutes: 70. (ii) 2 hours 45 minutes = ___ minutes: 165. (iii) 3 hours 15 minutes = ___ minutes: 195. (iv) 4 hours 20 minutes = ___ minutes: 260. (v) 75 minutes = ___ hour ___ minutes: 1 hour 15 minutes. (vi) 150 minutes = ___ hours ___ minutes: 2 hours 30 minutes. (vii) 220 minutes = ___ hours ___ minutes: 3 hours 40 minutes. (viii) 390 minutes = ___ hours ___ minutes: 6 hours 30 minutes. Why lines use each item's own numbers, like "2 × 60 = 120 and 120 + 45 = 165 minutes" for (ii) and "60 × 6 = 360 and 390 − 360 = 30, so 6 hours 30 minutes" for (viii). Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (minutes and seconds). Goal line: "Fill in the blanks in the double number line to complete the conversions." Chip: "6 blanks". Setup: Minutes and seconds, slider locked. Top line: 1 minute, ___, 5 minutes, 10 minutes, 15 minutes, ___, ___. Bottom line: 60 seconds, 120 seconds, ___, ___, ___, 1200 seconds, 1500 seconds (ticks at 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 minutes; a "× 5" arrow joins 1 minute to 5 minutes, a "× 60" arrow joins the lines). Guess: "Each minute adds how many seconds?" ("60", "100" or "10"). Answers: minutes 2, 20, 25; seconds 300, 600, 900. Why line: "1 minute is 60 seconds, so 5 × 60 = 300, 10 × 60 = 600 and 15 × 60 = 900." Then the goal line becomes "Complete the conversions." Chip: "7 conversions". Items and answers: (i) 320 seconds = ___ minutes ___ seconds: 5 minutes 20 seconds. (ii) 225 seconds = ___ minutes ___ seconds: 3 minutes 45 seconds. (iii) 700 seconds = ___ minutes ___ seconds: 11 minutes 40 seconds. (iv) 1,000 seconds = ___ minutes ___ seconds: 16 minutes 40 seconds. (v) 10 minutes 13 seconds = ___ seconds: 613. (vi) 4 minutes 8 seconds = ___ seconds: 248. (vii) 15 minutes 40 seconds = ___ seconds: 940. Why lines use each item's own numbers, like "60 × 16 = 960 and 1,000 − 960 = 40, so 16 minutes 40 seconds" for (iv) and "15 × 60 = 900 and 900 + 40 = 940 seconds" for (vii). Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3 (four subjects). Goal line: "Raghav studies Mathematics, English, Hindi, and The World Around Us subjects. He took 50 minutes to study each of the subjects. Find the total time taken in hours and minutes. Share your strategies with your class." Chip: "Total time ?". Setup: a bottom line of 0 to 240 minutes under a top line of 0 to 4 hours; the four books wait on the desk. Guess: "Will the four subjects take more than 3 hours?" ("Yes" or "No"). The child drags the books onto the line one after another (blocks of 50, 100, 150, 200 minutes), then writes "___ hours ___ minutes" with the pad. Result: "3 hours 20 minutes". Why line: "4 × 50 = 200 minutes, 60 × 3 = 180 and 200 − 180 = 20, so 3 hours 20 minutes." Other ways of adding are accepted. Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Every top tick sits over a bottom tick that is 60 times as far along: to the smaller unit the child multiplies by 60 and adds what is left over; back to the bigger unit the child finds how many whole blocks of 60 fit and keeps the short block.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the activity pill gets a tick and the strip gives the why line. A wrong answer gives a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line. Retry is free.
- Mistake: 100 used instead of 60 (110 minutes for 1 hour 10 minutes) -> "1 hour is 60 minutes, not 100. Each step on the line is 60." The "× 60" arrow pulses.
- Mistake: the extra minutes forgotten (120 for 2 hours 45 minutes) -> "You have the 2 hours. Now add the 45 minutes." Minutes above 59 (1 hour 75 minutes) -> "75 minutes is more than 1 hour. Cut a block of 60 first." The end-piece or a whole block pulses.
- Mistake: the wrong direction (390 × 60 for 390 minutes) -> "Minutes are smaller than hours, so there are fewer hours. Find how many 60s fit."
- Mistake in Challenge 3: three subjects counted (150 minutes) -> "Count the books on the desk: there are four."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Which unit is bigger, hours or minutes? Which line has the bigger numbers?" (2) visual clue: the "× 60" arrow lights up and the groups-of-60 strip appears. (3) almost the answer: the strip shows the whole blocks and the short block with its number replaced by "?".
- Edge cases: no minutes left (180 minutes is 3 hours 0 minutes, write 0).
7. Ending
- Each star is done when all its blanks and conversions are right. Hints are allowed.
- End screen: confetti falls here only. "Well done!" Remember: "1 hour is 60 minutes and 1 minute is 60 seconds." "To the smaller unit, multiply by 60 and add what is left over." "To the bigger unit, find how many whole 60s fit and keep the rest." Think and talk: "Why is 90 minutes not 1 hour 90 minutes?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: dark wooden desk top with lamp, pencil box and notebook (photo-style); cream paper tape; clear ruler with a brass handle and four plain school books (cut-outs). Lines, ticks, arrows, strip and pad are drawn in code.
- Language: English only; units are written in words.

tool_config.idea: Change one unit of time into the next on a double number line: hours into minutes, and minutes into seconds, where every step multiplies by 60, and back again by finding how many whole groups of 60 fit and what is left.
tool_config.title: Time Converter Line
tool_config.screen: The school notice board, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a long strip of paper pinned across the board carries a double number line, the largest thing on screen. The top line and the bottom line run side by side with aligned ticks, one tick below each tick. A mode switch above the strip reads Hours and minutes or Minutes and seconds: in the first mode the top line shows hours (0 to 12) and the bottom line minutes (0 to 720), in the second the top line shows minutes (0 to 25) and the bottom line seconds (0 to 1500). A bright slider with a handle sits on both lines at once and moves along them, snapping to a whole number on the top line, with the two numbers it points at shown in two read-out boxes. Curved arrows named × 60, × 2 and × 5 can be shown above the line with a button Show × 60. Blank ticks show a number box: tapping a box opens a large number pad. A groups of 60 strip under the bottom line can be switched on: it cuts the bottom number into whole blocks of 60 and shows the part that is left over as a short block. Controls: drag the slider, tap the mode switch, tap a blank box and type, tap Show × 60 and the groups of 60 switch, and tap Check. For a conversion card with hours and minutes, a sentence with blanks sits under the line, for example 1 hour 10 minutes = ___ minutes, and the student types the blanks. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (clears the boxes of this card), Reset (restores the line), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 7 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 7.
feedback: Sliding along the line shows both numbers at once and the arrow × 60: the bottom number is always 60 times the top number, and the read-out says so, for example 5 hours is 5 × 60 = 300 minutes.

media.teaching_notes: 1. (i): 1 hour = 60 minutes, so 1 hour 10 minutes is 60 + 10 = 70 minutes. 2. (ii): 2 hours = 2 × 60 = 120 minutes, and 120 + 45 = 165 minutes. 3. (iii): 3 hours = 3 × 60 = 180 minutes, and 180 + 15 = 195 minutes. 4. (iv): 4 hours = 4 × 60 = 240 minutes, and 240 + 20 = 260 minutes. 5. (v): 75 minutes: 60 minutes make 1 hour, and 75 − 60 = 15 minutes are left. So 1 hour 15 minutes. 6. (vi): 150 minutes: 60 × 2 = 120, and 150 − 120 = 30 minutes are left. So 2 hours 30 minutes. 7. (vii): 220 minutes: 60 × 3 = 180, and 220 − 180 = 40 minutes are left. So 3 hours 40 minutes. 8. (viii): 390 minutes: 60 × 6 = 360, and 390 − 360 = 30 minutes are left. So 6 hours 30 minutes. 9. Check: 3 × 60 + 40 = 220 and 6 × 60 + 30 = 390. Answer: (i): 70; (ii): 165; (iii): 195; (iv): 260 minutes. (v): 1 hour 15 minutes; (vi): 2 hours 30 minutes; (vii): 3 hours 40 minutes; (viii): 6 hours 30 minutes

content.text:
1. (i): $1$ hour $= 60$ minutes, so $1$ hour $10$ minutes is $60 + 10 = 70$ minutes.
2. (ii): $2$ hours $= 2 \times 60 = 120$ minutes, and $120 + 45 = 165$ minutes.
3. (iii): $3$ hours $= 3 \times 60 = 180$ minutes, and $180 + 15 = 195$ minutes.
4. (iv): $4$ hours $= 4 \times 60 = 240$ minutes, and $240 + 20 = 260$ minutes.
5. (v): $75$ minutes: $60$ minutes make $1$ hour, and $75 - 60 = 15$ minutes are left. So $1$ hour $15$ minutes.
6. (vi): $150$ minutes: $60 \times 2 = 120$, and $150 - 120 = 30$ minutes are left. So $2$ hours $30$ minutes.

media.title: Time Jumper
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Time Jumper
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S16.T16.C79.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Racing Seconds, time problems 4 to 10 (Jyoti, Ragini, the picnic, Raji, Alya, the lunch break and 08:35 PM) (developer only). Activities 1 to 4 use practice values.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that a time after or before a given time is found by hopping the hours first and then the minutes, that a.m. changes to p.m. at 12 noon, and that a new day begins after midnight.
- Out of scope: finding the time between two times, changing units, seconds.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- The school playground on a sunny morning: grey tarmac with a long chalk line of 11 hopscotch boxes, one for each hour, running left to right. This time line is the biggest thing on the stage (nearly the full stage width). Each box has its hour in big chalk digits and a tiny sun (a.m.) or moon (p.m.); chalk ticks inside mark every 10 minutes. A red flag stands at the start time with a child's red sneaker (photo-style cut-out) beside it.
- Under the line: a tray of four jump cards, "1 hour", "30 minutes", "10 minutes" and "5 minutes"; a round chalk switch "After" and "Before"; a small "Undo" arrow; a chip "Hopped: 0 minutes". Guided activities also show two read-outs, "12-hour" and "24-hour".
- Instruction line: "The flag is at 02:40 p.m. Hop forward 1 hour 35 minutes." The child is invited to drop a pebble first.
2. Scene and Objects
- The line always shows 11 boxes: the flag stands in the 2nd box on "After" cards and in the 10th box on "Before" cards. A bright chalk sun marks 12 noon, and the sun icons become moons after it. A thick chalk bar marks midnight and a band "Next day" follows it.
- Guided activities and Hint level 2 add small grey 24-hour counts under the boxes; in the Next day band they carry on 24, 25, 26.
3. Main Interaction
- Tap or drag a jump card onto the line: the shoe hops by that amount from where it stands (right when the switch says After, left when it says Before), a chalk arc is drawn and the Hopped chip adds up. Cards can be used again and again, at most 12 hops. "Undo" takes off the last hop; "Reset" takes off all hops.
- Guess: drag the pebble onto the box where the shoe will land.
- Answer: two wheels, hour 1 to 12 and minutes 00 to 55, and a switch "AM" with a sun and "PM" with a moon. No typing.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset" and "Check", which becomes "Next" when the chip is green.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "The flag is at 02:40 p.m. Hop forward 1 hour 35 minutes." Chip: "Land at ?". Setup: switch on After, read-outs and grey counts shown. Guess: the child drops the pebble on the box where the shoe will land. The child taps "1 hour", "30 minutes" and "5 minutes"; the shoe lands on 03:40 p.m., 04:10 p.m. and 04:15 p.m. and the read-outs follow. Result: the pebble turns green if it is on the 04 p.m. box. Why line: "02:40 p.m. plus 1 hour is 03:40 p.m., 03:40 p.m. to 04:00 p.m. is 20 minutes, and 35 − 20 = 15 minutes are left, so 04:15 p.m." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "The flag is at 07:50 p.m. Hop back 2 hours 20 minutes." Chip: "Land at ?". Setup: the switch starts on After; hopping that way gets the note "The time before is earlier. Turn the switch to Before and hop left." Guess: the pebble. The child taps "1 hour" twice and "10 minutes" twice; the shoe lands on 06:50 p.m., 05:50 p.m., 05:40 p.m. and 05:30 p.m. Why line: "07:50 p.m. minus 2 hours is 05:50 p.m., and 05:50 p.m. minus 20 minutes is 05:30 p.m." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "The flag is at 11:25 a.m. Hop forward 1 hour 40 minutes. Watch 12 noon." Chip: "Land at ?". Setup: read-outs and counts hidden. Guess: "Will the shoe land in the morning or in the afternoon?" ("a.m." or "p.m."). The child hops and writes the landing time with the wheels. Result: "01:05 p.m."; the chalk sun at noon becomes a moon as the shoe passes it. Why line: "In 24-hour time, 11:25 hours plus 1 hour 40 minutes is 13:05 hours, and 13 − 12 = 1, so 01:05 p.m." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "The flag is at 11:10 p.m. Hop forward 3 hours 20 minutes. Watch midnight." Chip: "Land at ?". Setup as in Activity 3. Guess: "Will the shoe land today or on the next day?" The child hops and writes the landing time. Result: "02:30 a.m." and the Next day band lights up. Why line: "In 24-hour time, 23:10 hours plus 3 hours 20 minutes is 26:30 hours, and 26 − 24 = 2, so 02:30 a.m. the next day." Help: independent.
- Practice: none.
- Star Challenge 1 (the time problems). Chip: "5 problems". Setup: the flag stands at the time in the story (for Ragini at the finish, 09:40 PM); the child sets the switch, hops and writes the time in the book's style, with AM or PM. Guess for each: the pebble on the box where the shoe will land. Goal lines, one at a time, with the answer and the why line: 1 "Jyoti went to play at 06:15 PM. She came back after 1 hour 45 minutes. At what time did she reach home?" 08:00 PM: "06:15 PM plus 1 hour is 07:15 PM, and 45 more minutes reach 08:00 PM." 2 "Ragini took 1 hour 10 minutes to do her homework. She finished it at 09:40 PM. What time did she start?" 08:30 PM: "09:40 PM minus 1 hour is 08:40 PM, and 08:40 PM minus 10 minutes is 08:30 PM." 3 "A group of children left for a picnic at 08:30 AM. They returned after 4 hours and 10 minutes. At what time did they return?" 12:40 PM: "08:30 AM plus 4 hours is 12:30 PM, the clock passes 12 noon so AM changes to PM, and 10 more minutes reach 12:40 PM." 4 "Raji started her homework at 06:00 PM. She finished her homework in 1 hour 30 minutes. At what time did she finish?" 07:30 PM: "06:00 PM plus 1 hour is 07:00 PM, and 30 more minutes reach 07:30 PM." 5 "Alya goes out to play at 05:30 PM and comes back after 1 hour 10 minutes. At what time does she come back?" 06:40 PM: "05:30 PM plus 1 hour is 06:30 PM, and 10 more minutes reach 06:40 PM." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (noon and midnight). Chip: "2 problems". Setup and guess as in Star Challenge 1. Goal lines: 1 "If the lunch break of a school starts at 12:30 PM and ends in 35 minutes, what time will lunch end?" 01:05 PM: "12:30 PM plus 30 minutes is 01:00 PM, and 5 more minutes reach 01:05 PM." 2 "It is 08:35 PM right now. What time will it be after 8 hours and 25 minutes?" 05:00 AM, with the shoe in the Next day band: "In 24-hour time, 20:35 hours plus 8 hours 25 minutes is 29:00 hours, and 29 − 24 = 5, so it is 05:00 AM the next day." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Hopping the hours first and then the minutes to the next whole hour makes any time problem a few easy jumps, forward for a time after and left for a time before. The sun becoming a moon at noon shows why a.m. changes to p.m., and the Next day band shows that after midnight the count starts again.
6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the activity pill gets a tick and the strip gives the why line. A wrong answer gives a red strip, a small shake and one friendly line. Retry is free.
- Mistake: the hour not moved on when the minutes reach 60 (07:00 PM for 08:00 PM in problem 1 of Star Challenge 1) -> "60 minutes make 1 hour, so the hour goes up by 1." The landing box and the next box pulse.
- Mistake: the wrong way (hopping forward for "What time did she start?") -> "She finished at 09:40 PM, so she started earlier. Hop left." The switch pulses.
- Mistake: a.m. or p.m. wrong after noon -> "The shoe passed 12 noon, so the sun became a moon: it is PM." Past midnight (05:00 PM for Star Challenge 2, problem 2) -> "You went past midnight. A new day has begun, so it is AM again." The noon mark or the Next day band pulses.
- Mistake: the hops do not match the story -> "Your jumps add up to 1 hour 40 minutes. The story says 1 hour 45 minutes." The Hopped chip pulses.
- Mistake: the hour kept at 12 for problem 1 of Star Challenge 2 -> "The 12-hour clock goes 11, 12, then 01. The hour after 12 is 1." The hour box on the line pulses.
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Are you finding the time after or the time before? Which way does the shoe hop?" (2) visual clue: a ghost shoe hops the hours first and stops, and a short chalk bar shows the minutes to the next whole hour. (3) almost the answer: the ghost shoe also hops to the next whole hour and shows "? minutes still to go".
- Edge cases: a landing exactly on a whole hour (07:00 PM) reads ":00"; the line never lets the shoe hop off its ends; a hop that lands exactly on 12 noon or midnight changes the sun or the band at once.
7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when all five times are right, Star Challenge 2 when both are right. Hints are allowed.
- End screen: confetti falls here only. "Well done!" Remember: "Hop the hours first, then the minutes to the next whole hour, then the rest." "Minutes stop at 59: after 59 the hour goes up by 1." "At 12 noon a.m. changes to p.m., and after midnight a new day begins." Think and talk: "You find a start time by hopping back. How can you hop forward to check it?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: school playground tarmac (photo-style); red sneaker and red flag (cut-outs); chalk jump cards and a pebble (cut-outs). The chalk boxes, ticks, sun and moon icons, arcs, bars and wheels are drawn in code.
- Language: English only. The book's time problems keep the book's style ("06:15 PM"); everything else has a leading zero and "a.m." or "p.m.".

tool_config.idea: Find the time after, or before, a time by hopping along a time line, the hours first and then the minutes up to the next whole hour, and see the a.m. and p.m. change at 12 noon and a new day begin after midnight.
tool_config.title: Time Jumper
tool_config.screen: The school playground, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a long hopscotch line chalked on the ground is a time line and is the largest thing on screen. The line has a tall tick for every whole hour and 5 small ticks of 5 minutes between them, with the hours labelled; the left part of the line has a sun and the label a.m., the right part has a moon and the label p.m., 12 noon has a bright marker, and after 12 midnight a band named Next day starts. A small flag stands at the start time and a child's shoe hops from the flag to the landing time. Jump cards sit in a tray under the line: 1 hour, 30 minutes, 10 minutes, 5 minutes and 1 minute, each with a Forward and a Back side. A read-out beside the line shows the landing time in the 12-hour format (hh:mm a.m. or p.m.) and a second read-out shows the 24-hour time (hh:mm hours); a small clock with a blue hour hand and an orange minute hand follows the landing time. Controls: drag a jump card onto the line (the shoe hops by that much and the landing time updates), tap Undo to take the last jump off, tap Forward or Back to choose the direction of the card, type the end time with a large number pad, and tap Check. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (returns the shoe to the start of this card), Reset (clears every jump), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 7 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 7.
feedback: A jump makes the shoe hop and the landing time update at once, with the 24-hour time beside it, so the student sees what each hop does.
A wrong end time gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red: from 07:15 PM, 45 minutes reach 08:00 PM, not 07:60 PM, because minutes on a clock never go past 59.
When the shoe passes 12 noon the a.m. sun changes to the p.m. moon with a short note, and when it passes midnight the Next day band lights up and the 24-hour read-out goes back to 00:00 hours.
A time typed with the wrong a.m. or p.m. gets a note that points to the sun and moon on the line: after 12 noon the time is p.m.
A backward hop typed as a forward hop gets a note: the time before is earlier on the line, so the shoe hops to the left.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are done, the seven time problems of the book are answered correctly, and the last card is finished without a bottom-out hint.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): the flag is at 02:10 p.m. Hop forward 1 hour 35 minutes with an hour card and minute cards. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 03:45 p.m., because 02:10 p.m. plus 1 hour is 03:10 p.m. and 03:10 p.m. plus 35 minutes is 03:45 p.m.

Card 2 (practice values): the flag is at 07:50 p.m. Hop back 2 hours 20 minutes. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 05:30 p.m., because 07:50 p.m. minus 2 hours is 05:50 p.m. and 05:50 p.m. minus 20 minutes is 05:30 p.m.

Card 3 (practice values): the flag is at 11:25 a.m. Hop forward 1 hour 50 minutes and watch 12 noon. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 01:15 p.m., because 11:25 a.m. plus 1 hour is 12:25 p.m. and 12:25 p.m. plus 50 minutes is 01:15 p.m. The a.m. changed to p.m. at 12 noon.

Card 4 (practice values): the flag is at 11:10 p.m. Hop forward 3 hours 20 minutes and watch midnight. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 02:30 a.m. the next day, because 23:10 hours plus 3 hours 20 minutes is 26:30 hours, and 26 − 24 = 2.

Card 5 (practice values): the flag is at 04:40 p.m. and the shoe has to land on 06:15 p.m. Choose the jump cards. Answer: 1 hour 35 minutes, for example 20 minutes to 05:00 p.m., 1 hour to 06:00 p.m. and 15 minutes to 06:15 p.m., and 20 + 15 = 35 minutes.

Challenge: 'Jyoti went to play at 06:15 PM. She came back after 1 hour 45 minutes. At what time did she reach home?' 'Ragini took 1 hour 10 minutes to do her homework. She finished it at 09:40 PM. What time did she start?' 'A group of children left for a picnic at 08:30 AM. They returned after 4 hours and 10 minutes. At what time did they return?' 'Raji started her homework at 06:00 PM. She finished her homework in 1 hour 30 minutes. At what time did she finish?' 'Alya goes out to play at 05:30 PM and comes back after 1 hour 10 minutes. At what time does she come back?' Answers: 08:00 PM, 08:30 PM, 12:40 PM, 07:30 PM and 06:40 PM.

Challenge: 'If the lunch break of a school starts at 12:30 PM and ends in 35 minutes, what time will lunch end?' 'It is 08:35 PM right now. What time will it be after 8 hours and 25 minutes?' Answers: 01:05 PM, and 05:00 AM the next day, because 20:35 hours plus 8 hours 25 minutes is 29:00 hours and 29 − 24 = 5.

hint_ladder.text: Are you finding the time after or the time before? Which way along the line does the shoe hop?
Hop the hours first. Then ask: how many minutes to the next whole hour, and how many minutes are left?
Drag the hour card first, then the minute cards. Check where the shoe lands after the hour card, then add the minutes that are left.
Worked step on a practice card: 02:45 p.m. plus 1 hour is 03:45 p.m., and 15 minutes reach 04:00 p.m., so the first jumps are 1 hour and 15 minutes. Do the same with your card.

student_does: Look at the flag at 03:20 p.m. and one jump of 1 hour, as in the video. Say where the shoe lands and what is left to add.
Drag jump cards to find the time after a time, then the time before a time, then a time after that passes 12 noon, and one that passes midnight (practice values).
Solve the book's time problems by hopping and type each time.
